outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 settles, or moves the bound in, any dimension of the question. The in-window items are a 23 May 2025 seminar abstract on Coxeter-trisected 'Pythagorean simplices' that states no result for general simplices, two 2025-2026 hyperbolic one-loop papers whose orthoscheme decompositions are signed rather than dissections, and a 2026 paper using signed orthoscheme decompositions as a tool for a spherical valuation theorem. Wikipedia (fetched; shown as last edited 27 December 2025) still describes the problem as unsolved for dimensions above five.
problem_asks: (1) For every dimension d, whether every d-dimensional simplex can be dissected into finitely many orthoschemes (the frozen statement: 'is it possible for simplices of every dimension?'). (2) The sharper form the Wikipedia article gives as Hadwiger's 1956 conjecture: whether there is one function f such that every d-simplex dissects into at most f(d) orthoschemes, so that the count depends only on the dimension. (3) The statement names no geometry; it reads as Euclidean simplices. The article also reports Euclidean-type results in d=3 and d=5 that it says extend to spherical and hyperbolic geometry, which the statement does not ask. (4) Not asked, but noted by the article: a positive answer would mean every convex polytope dissects into orthoschemes. Known cases per Wikipedia: d=2 (every triangle into at most two right triangles, Hadwiger 1956); d=3 (every tetrahedron into at most 12, Lenhard 1960, optimal by Böhm 1980); d=4 (at most 500, Tschirpke 1993); d=5 (a finite bound, roughly 12.5 million, Tschirpke 1994). Wikipedia states the conjecture 'remains unproven for all dimensions greater than five', so the open part is every d >= 6, for both the finite-count and the uniform-bound forms.

events.what_happened: Hugo Hadwiger posed the question in 'Ungelöste Probleme', Elemente der Mathematik 11 (1956) 109-110, as cited by Wikipedia's dissection article and its Schläfli orthoscheme article. Wikipedia attributes to this source the d=2 fact that every triangle dissects into at most two right triangles, by dropping the altitude from its widest angle onto its longest side. A bibliographic record I opened (EuDML doc 140668) lists a different 'Ungelöste Probleme' by H. Hadwiger in Elem. Math. 12 (1957) 85-86; whether that is another installment of the same column is not resolved. The original column was not read.
events.delivers: Poses the question: whether a function f(d) exists such that every d-simplex dissects into at most f(d) orthoschemes, and whether that would make every convex polytope dissectable into orthoschemes. Per Wikipedia, it also yields the d=2 case, every triangle into at most two right triangles. Nothing for d >= 3.
events.remains: Every d >= 3, in both the finite-count form and the uniform-bound form.
events.directly_checkable: The d=2 statement is elementary: drop the altitude from the widest angle of a triangle; the two pieces are right triangles.
events.direction: Poses the question. The only consequence stated is the d=2 case, which goes the 'yes' way.

events.what_happened: H.-Chr. Lenhard, 'Zerlegung von Tetraedern in Orthogonaltetraeder', Elemente der Mathematik 15 (1960) 106-107 (MR 0116226). Per Wikipedia, every tetrahedron can be dissected into at most 12 orthoschemes, by a more involved construction than the altitude method, which does not always work. The original was not read: the Digizeitschriften link I tried returned 404, and the search results gave no other scan.
events.delivers: For d=3 (Euclidean tetrahedra, as Wikipedia states it): every tetrahedron dissects into at most 12 orthoschemes, a uniform bound. Covers every tetrahedron. Says nothing for d >= 4.

checked_by.qualification: Author of the optimality paper cited by Wikipedia for the 12 bound; a later specialist in orthoscheme dissections of tetrahedra.
checked_by.what_they_did: Per Wikipedia, showed that 12 cannot be lowered (there exist tetrahedra needing at least 12 orthoschemes) and extended Lenhard's result to three-dimensional spherical and hyperbolic geometry. The original was not read.

events.direction: Goes the 'yes' way for d=3, with an explicit uniform count of 12.

events.what_happened: Böhm (1980), 'Zur vollständigen Zerlegung der euklidischen und nichteuklidischen Tetraeder in Orthogonal-Tetraeder', Martin-Luther-Universität Halle-Wittenberg report (9), 29-54 (MR 0579516). Per Wikipedia: shows that there exist tetrahedra that cannot be dissected into fewer than 12 orthoschemes, so 12 is optimal, and extends Lenhard's result to three-dimensional spherical and hyperbolic geometry. The original was not read.
events.delivers: For d=3: the uniform count 12 for tetrahedra is sharp (per Wikipedia's lower-bound statement). Per Wikipedia, the 12-orthoscheme upper bound is also extended to three-dimensional spherical and hyperbolic tetrahedra. Nothing for d >= 4.
events.doubts: Only Wikipedia's statements were read. The lower-bound claim is reported, not checked; the report itself was not read, and I found no later check of it in what I read.
events.direction: Goes the 'yes' way for d=3 (count 12 is best possible), and extends the d=3 picture to non-Euclidean 3-space per Wikipedia.
events.object: Per Wikipedia, 'there exist tetrahedra that cannot be dissected into fewer than 12 orthoschemes'. Which tetrahedra these are, and whether the argument is explicit or non-constructive, was not read.

events.what_happened: H. E. Debrunner, 'Dissecting orthoschemes into orthoschemes', Geometriae Dedicata 33 (1990) 123-152 (DOI 10.1007/BF00183080, MR 1050606). Per Wikipedia: every orthoscheme dissects into d or d+1 smaller orthoschemes (Wikipedia also cites Brandts, Korotov and Křížek 2007). A Kellerhals text (search snippet, not opened) describes Debrunner's dissection of a d-orthoscheme into d+1 orthoschemes, used to show that for odd d > 3 the hyperbolic scissors congruence group is generated by 2-asymptotic orthoschemes. The original was not read.
events.delivers: Dissects an orthoscheme, not an arbitrary simplex, into d or d+1 orthoschemes. Because the input is already an orthoscheme, this is a neighbouring statement, not a step toward dissecting a general simplex.
events.remains: The whole question for simplices that are not orthoschemes, in every d.
events.doubts: The original paper was not read; the d or d+1 count is taken from Wikipedia and from a garbled OCR passage in a Kellerhals preprint search snippet.
events.direction: Neutral to the question: it fixes piece counts for orthoschemes, not for general simplices.

events.what_happened: K. Tschirpke, 'On the dissection of simplices into orthoschemes', Geometriae Dedicata 46 (1993) 313-329 (DOI 10.1007/BF01263622, MR 1220122, Zbl 0780.52016). Per Wikipedia: in four dimensions, at most 500 orthoschemes are needed. The paper was not read: the DOI resolved to a Springer login redirect that my fetch did not follow. A search summary, unverified, also mentions a 1993 Jena dissertation with a German title on five-dimensional simplices in constant curvature.
events.delivers: For d=4: a uniform count of at most 500 orthoschemes for a 4-simplex, as Wikipedia reports it. Wikipedia's d=4 sentence does not say whether the setting is Euclidean.
events.remains: Every d >= 5, with d=5 handled by the next event.
events.doubts: The d=4 figure rests on Wikipedia alone; the paper was not read, and the geometry is not confirmed.
events.direction: Goes the 'yes' way for d=4, with an explicit bound of 500.

events.what_happened: K. Tschirpke, 'The dissection of five-dimensional simplices into orthoschemes', Beiträge zur Algebra und Geometrie 35 (1994) 1-11 (MR 1287191, Zbl 0806.52012). Per Wikipedia: every five-dimensional simplex needs a finite number of orthoschemes, 'roughly bounded as at most 12.5 million', and the article says this also holds in spherical and hyperbolic geometry. The Schläfli orthoscheme article states that the conjecture is proven for five or fewer dimensions, citing this paper. The paper was not read. A search listing gives 1995 for it, which conflicts with 1994.
events.delivers: For d=5: a finite (uniform) orthoscheme count for Euclidean 5-simplices, roughly 12.5 million per Wikipedia; Wikipedia says it also holds for spherical and hyperbolic 5-simplices. The bound is given only as 'roughly'.
events.doubts: The paper was not read. Its year conflicts between sources (1994 in Wikipedia and the bibliographic records I saw; 1995 in one search summary). The bound is Wikipedia's rough figure.
events.direction: Goes the 'yes' way for d=5.

events.what_happened: J. Brandts, S. Korotov and M. Křížek, 'Dissection of the path-simplex in R^n into n path-subsimplices', Helsinki University of Technology / Aalto report A496 (2006), published in Linear Algebra and its Applications 421 (2007) 382-393 (DOI 10.1016/j.laa.2006.10.010, MR 2294350). Per search-result abstracts and Wikipedia's citation: a path-simplex (an orthoscheme) is dissected into n path-subsimplices, generalizing Coxeter's trisection of a path-tetrahedron, with a recursive self-similar refinement. The report PDF returned a compressed binary through my fetch and could not be read; the journal article was not reached.
events.revisions: Report A496 (2006); journal version Linear Algebra Appl. 421 (2007).
events.delivers: Restricted to one path-simplex (orthoscheme) subdivided into n orthoschemes. Does not dissect a general simplex.
events.remains: The whole question for simplices that are not orthoschemes, in every d.
events.doubts: Only search-result abstracts and Wikipedia's citation were read; the construction was not checked.
events.direction: Neutral to the question: fixes an orthoscheme-into-orthoscheme count of n.

events.what_happened: N. J. A. Sloane and V. A. Vaishampayan (on Schöbi's 1985 three-piece dissection), 'Generalizations of Schöbi's Tetrahedral Dissection', arXiv:0710.3857 (October 2007, from the arXiv identifier; not opened). Per search summaries only: extends Schöbi's three-piece cut of the 3D Hill simplex, which Schöbi calls an orthoscheme, to n dimensions, dissecting it into an n-dimensional brick using at most n! pieces, with O(n^2) map complexity. The pieces here are bricks, not orthoschemes.
events.delivers: Dissects a Hill-type orthoscheme into bricks (parallelepipeds), not into orthoschemes. Discounted: a different target and a different piece type.
events.doubts: Not opened; the description comes from search summaries.
events.direction: Not about the question's direction; it changes the target shape.

events.what_happened: J. Brandts, S. Korotov, M. Křížek and J. Šolc, 'On nonobtuse simplicial partitions', SIAM Review 51(2) (2009) 317-335 (DOI 10.1137/060669073). Per Wikipedia's citation, Conjecture 23 (p. 327) is the source the dissection article cites for the orthoscheme question. The survey was not read: the SIAM page returned 403. A precursor, HUT report A503 'On acute and nonobtuse simplicial partitions' (2006), was seen only as a search listing; its PDF was unreadable through my fetch.
events.revisions: Precursor HUT / Aalto report A503 (2006), not read.
events.delivers: Nothing settled in what I read. As a survey, it restates the question as open in 2009, per Wikipedia's citation of Conjecture 23.
events.doubts: Conjecture 23's exact wording was not read, so whether it is this problem or a nonobtuse variant is not confirmed. A search summary notes that the SIAM Review abstract is about acute and nonobtuse partitions with path-simplices.
events.direction: Neutral; a status signal that the problem was open in 2009.

events.what_happened: Florestan Brunck (McGill University), seminar 'Non-Obtuse Dissection of Tetrahedra', 19 September 2018, Burnside Hall room 1104 (McGill event page, opened). The page's abstract, as the fetch tool gave it, frames Hadwiger's 1956 open conjecture as whether every d-simplex dissects into non-obtuse d-simplices, and reports 'a constructive answer in dimension 3', with '28 orthoschemes are sufficient to dissect any tetrahedron'. No write-up, arXiv version or journal article was found in any search.
events.delivers: Ambiguous from the abstract. Reading (a): the 28 pieces are orthoschemes, a d=3 uniform count weaker than Lenhard's 12, so no gain for this problem. Reading (b): the 28 pieces are non-obtuse simplices, a d=3 answer to the non-obtuse variant, which is a different question. The abstract does not say which.
events.remains: Every d >= 4 under either reading. Under reading (a), d=3 is already covered by Lenhard (1960).
events.time_since_posted: about 8 years, with no written version found
events.doubts: Only the seminar abstract is available. No write-up was found. The event page frames the problem in non-obtuse terms, and the count 28 is larger than Lenhard's older 12 for the orthoscheme reading.
events.direction: Goes the 'yes' way in either reading (a finite constructive count for every tetrahedron), but for a different piece type in reading (b).

events.what_happened: István Lénárt, 'The Right Triangle as the Simplex in 2D Euclidean Space, Generalized to n Dimensions', Rényi Institute talk listed as 16 December 2022 (video listing, opened). Per the listing: right-triangle-type 'Pythagorean' simplices exist in every n-dimensional Euclidean space, and a generalized Pythagorean theorem gives the volume from the legs without the Cayley-Menger determinant. The listing does not mention dissection or Hadwiger's conjecture.
events.delivers: Existence and a volume formula for orthoscheme-type simplices in every dimension. No dissection of any simplex.
events.doubts: Only the listing was read. The talk is background to the 2025 talk below.
events.direction: Not about the question's direction.

events.what_happened: Lecheng Ren, Marcus Spradlin, Cristian Vergu and Anastasia Volovich, 'One-loop Integrals from Volumes of Orthoschemes', arXiv:2306.04630 (v1 7 June 2023; v2 revised 12 April 2024 per the abstract page). It evaluates one-loop Feynman integrals from hyperbolic orthoscheme volumes, with the simplex triangulated into orthoschemes. The body, read through a targeted fetch, says the triangulation 'is not a dissection since some components may lie outside the original simplex', that such components 'contribute to the total volume with a minus sign', and that 'It is a conjecture of Hadwiger that any simplex can be dissected into orthoschemes', so the question is treated as open in 2023.
events.revisions: v1 7 Jun 2023; v2 12 Apr 2024 (after the frozen revision; content of v2 not examined beyond the date).
events.delivers: Nothing on the question. States a signed volume decomposition of hyperbolic simplices arising in one-loop integrals, which the paper itself says is not a dissection.
events.doubts: The statements about signs and non-dissection come from a targeted fetch of the HTML body, not a verbatim full read.
events.direction: Not a step toward the 'yes' or 'no' direction; the paper treats the question as open.

events.what_happened: István Lénárt, 'The Coxeter Trisection and the Hadwiger Conjecture in Multidimensional Spaces', Budapest Big Combinatorics + Geometry Seminar, HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute, 23 May 2025 (event page, opened). The abstract as listed: an n-dimensional simplex with one hypotenuse and n-1 legs forming an orthogonal edge path (so an orthoscheme); an existence proof for these shapes; an algebraic proof of Coxeter's trisection of a quadrirectangular tetrahedron into three smaller tetrahedra of the same type, generalized to n dimensions; and 'Finally, I analyze the connection between the Coxeter partition and the Hadwiger conjecture regarding the partition of the simplex into a finite number of orthoschemes, which I call Pythagorean simplices.' No slides, notes, or arXiv version were found.
events.delivers: As listed, a claimed n-dimensional generalization of one specific Coxeter trisection (of a quadrirectangular tetrahedron, a special orthoscheme, into three pieces of its own type). The Hadwiger link is described as an 'analysis' with no stated result. No theorem for general simplices is stated.
events.remains: The whole question for general simplices in every d; the abstract claims no dissection of an arbitrary simplex.
events.time_since_posted: about 16 months, with no write-up or public discussion found
events.doubts: Only the seminar listing was read. Whether the 'analysis' of the Hadwiger connection yields any statement about general simplices is not visible from the abstract.
events.direction: Not clear from the abstract. The trisection is a special case inside the orthoscheme family; no general dissection is claimed.

events.what_happened: Claude Duhr and Paul Mork, 'Analytic results for one-loop integrals in dimensional regularisation', arXiv:2512.14363 (submitted 16 December 2025; one version listed). A method for one-loop triangle, box and pentagon integrals via multiple polylogarithms, using the volumes of hyperbolic simplices. Section 2.3, 'Dissecting simplices into orthoschemes', states that 'The decomposition of a simplex in H^{N-1} into a union of orthoschemes is not unique', and that the recursive projection 'results in a decomposition of the simplex S_Q into (N-1)! orthoschemes'. The paper's eq. (9), as read through the fetch, is a signed sum over the pieces with a sign factor, which the text says is needed because projected vertices 'might lie outside of the face they were projected to'. A search summary had described this as a dissection; the paper's own text does not support that reading.
events.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2025 is the only version listed on the abstract page.
events.delivers: For a hyperbolic simplex S_Q arising from a one-loop Gram matrix Q: a recursive, signed decomposition into (N-1)! orthoschemes, with the volume as a signed sum. Not a dissection in the question's sense, by the paper's own sign factor. Nothing claimed for Euclidean simplices or for a dimension-uniform bound.
events.remains: The whole question: a genuine dissection of any simplex (Euclidean, or hyperbolic without signs) into finitely many orthoschemes, in every dimension.
events.doubts: The decomposition is signed, by the paper's own eq. (9) and sign factor, so it is not a dissection. The only verbatim text I checked is the HTML version, which I read through the acknowledgements. The PDF is compressed and was not readable. The claim 'a union of orthoschemes' in the same section is the paper's wording and is not reconciled with the signed sum in the text.
events.direction: Signed. Cuts toward a finite count for hyperbolic simplices in a weaker, signed sense; not a dissection and not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: Paul Mork, 'Recursive construction of scalar one-loop integrals in dimensional regularisation', arXiv:2607.16416 (submitted 17 July 2026; one version; report BONN-TH/2026-15). The abstract gives a recursion for dimensionally regularised scalar one-loop integrals from Schläfli's differential formula and the ε=0 volumes of hyperbolic simplices; the abstract does not mention orthoschemes. The body, read through the HTML version, uses orthoscheme dissections as cited input. It says 'Every hyperbolic simplex can be decomposed algorithmically into a finite collection of orthoschemes', citing refs [13] (Davydychev and Delbourgo) and [36] (Duhr and Mork, arXiv:2512.14363), and says in §2.4 that this dissection is 'signed in general' (as read through the fetch tool). The acknowledgements thank Claude Duhr, a human supervisor.
events.revisions: v1 17 Jul 2026 is the only version listed on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing on the question. It restates the signed hyperbolic orthoscheme decomposition of Duhr and Mork as an input to its own recursion.
events.doubts: My first check read only the abstract and missed the orthoscheme content in the body; the body was read in two parts (HTML). The statement 'every hyperbolic simplex can be decomposed' is flagged in the paper itself as signed in general.
events.direction: Not a step toward a direction for the question. Its one orthoscheme-decomposition statement is explicitly signed.

events.what_happened: Martin Lotz, 'Hadwiger's classification theorem on the sphere via signed orthoscheme decompositions', arXiv:2609.17437 (v1 15 September 2026; one version listed). Per the abstract: an elementary combinatorial proof of the spherical Hadwiger theorem (continuous rotation-invariant valuations on closed convex cones in R^n are linear combinations of the conic intrinsic volumes), using a signed orthoscheme decomposition as a proof tool. This is Hadwiger's valuation theorem, not the Hadwiger dissection conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 15 Sep 2026 is the only version listed on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing on the question. A valuation theorem on spherical cones; the orthoscheme decomposition is a signed internal tool, not a dissection of simplices.
events.doubts: Only the abstract page was read; the PDF was not read, so its acknowledgements and any AI statement are unchecked.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different theorem with the same name.

events.what_happened: Sergey Norin and Raphael Steiner, 'A Proof of the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture', arXiv:2610.05291 (v1 4 October 2026). A graph-theory result: graphs with no K_t minor are properly colourable with at most C·t colours, for a universal constant C. Not about simplices or dissections. Recorded only because it carries the Hadwiger name and an AI attribution. The abstract page states: 'The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra, following the directions by the authors.' This is a different question and settles nothing here.
events.revisions: v1 4 Oct 2026 is the only version listed on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing on orthoscheme dissection. A graph-colouring theorem.
events.doubts: Only the abstract page was read. The paper is about graphs, so its AI attribution is recorded only as a neighbouring-name event.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different problem with the same name.

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, found the proof of the linear Hadwiger conjecture for graphs, 'following the directions by the authors'. This is a graph-colouring theorem, not this problem; the entry is here for the audit of neighbouring events.
systems.basis_quote: The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra, following the directions by the authors.

disputes.summary: Hadwiger's 1956 'Ungelöste Probleme' is cited as Elem. Math. 11 (1956) 109-110 by Wikipedia and the Schläfli orthoscheme article; EuDML lists a 'Ungelöste Probleme' by H. Hadwiger in Elem. Math. 12 (1957) 85-86. Not resolved from what I could open.
Tschirpke's five-dimensional paper is dated 1994 by Wikipedia and the bibliographic records seen, but 1995 in one search listing. The 1994 date is recorded.

Duhr and Mork (2025) and Mork (2026) describe an algorithmic decomposition of every hyperbolic simplex into finitely many orthoschemes ('decomposition', and in §2.3 'a union of orthoschemes'), while their own eq. (9) and §2.4 treat it as signed, with pieces that can lie outside. A search summary called it a dissection. The record follows the papers' own statement that it is signed.

Brunck's 2018 abstract says 28 orthoschemes suffice for any tetrahedron, but frames the problem as a non-obtuse dissection. Whether the 28 pieces are orthoschemes or non-obtuse simplices is not settled by the abstract.

summary: The problem asks whether every simplex in every dimension can be dissected into finitely many orthoschemes, and Wikipedia's dissection article sharpens this to Hadwiger's 1956 conjecture on a dimension-only bound f(d). Wikipedia (fetched) reports the known cases: d=2 (Hadwiger 1956), d=3 with a uniform count of 12 (Lenhard 1960, shown optimal by Böhm 1980), d=4 with at most 500 (Tschirpke 1993), d=5 with a finite count (Tschirpke 1994, roughly 12.5 million), and says the conjecture remains unproven for every dimension above five. I searched for a post-January-2024 result that settles or moves the bound in any dimension and found none. Events in the window: (i) the 23 May 2025 Lénárt seminar, whose abstract claims an n-dimensional generalization of Coxeter's trisection of one special orthoscheme and says it 'analyze[s] the connection' to the Hadwiger conjecture, with no stated result for general simplices and no write-up found; (ii) Duhr and Mork (16 December 2025) and Mork (17 July 2026), whose text describes a decomposition of every hyperbolic simplex into finitely many orthoschemes, with (N-1)! pieces for S_Q, but whose own eq. (9) and §2.4 make it a signed sum, so it is not a dissection; Ren et al. (2023) say explicitly that their triangulation 'is not a dissection' and call Hadwiger's question open; (iii) Lotz (15 September 2026) uses signed orthoscheme decompositions as a tool for a spherical valuation theorem, a different question; (iv) Norin and Steiner (4 October 2026), a graph-colouring theorem with an AI attribution to 'GPT-6 Astra', a different question. The 2018 Brunck seminar, the only other item with a numerical result for tetrahedra, is ambiguous: its 28 pieces may be orthoschemes, in which case it is weaker than Lenhard's 12, or non-obtuse simplices, a different variant; no write-up was found. AI: no source bearing on this problem names a system. The AI-credited items I found concern other problems: Norin and Steiner (graph colouring, opened); a Wang and Wu spherical Hadwiger covering proof reported as made with OpenAI Codex (search summary only, not opened); the Illingworth and Steiner dominating-Hadwiger disproof credited to GPT-6 Astra (MathWorld summary, not opened); an OpenAI unit-distance announcement of May 2026 (search summary, not opened); and a majority-of-three learning-theory paper whose appendix describes GPT-5.5 Pro use (opened; unrelated). No human has publicly checked any in-window result on this problem, and the original 1956-2009 papers were not read; their statements come from Wikipedia and secondary records.
competing_reading: Read the Duhr-Mork and Mork decompositions as genuine dissections: §2.3 says 'a decomposition of the simplex S_Q into (N-1)! orthoschemes' and Mork says 'Every hyperbolic simplex can be decomposed algorithmically into a finite collection of orthoschemes'. If taken at face value and applied to all hyperbolic simplices, that would be a finite, dimension-bounded orthoscheme count for a non-Euclidean version of the problem dated December 2025, a live event for the existence part. The papers' own sign factor (eq. 9, and 'signed in general' in §2.4) is the strongest reason against this reading, and Ren et al. (2023) draw the same line. Second, read Brunck's 28 as a dissection into orthoschemes: then it is a constructive d=3 count, but a weaker one than Lenhard's 12, so it moves nothing on this problem.
what_would_settle_it: (a) For the hyperbolic decompositions: the statement and proof of the algorithm in reference [33] of arXiv:2512.14363, and whether any sign in eq. (9) is negative for a genuine simplex; the question is whether the pieces have disjoint interiors and cover S_Q. (b) For Brunck 2018: the talk's slides, a write-up, or the full verbatim abstract, to see whether the pieces are 'orthoschemes' or 'non-obtuse'. (c) For Lénárt 2025: the slides, a recording or an arXiv preprint, to see what 'analyze the connection' actually proves for general simplices. (d) For the classical bounds: the originals of Lenhard (1960), Böhm (1980), Tschirpke (1993) and (1994), which I could not open, to confirm the 12, 500 and 12.5-million figures and their geometric setting. (e) For the AI question: the authors' own account of any AI use in a new in-window paper that claims a dissection of general simplices. None has been found.

events.credibility_reason: Seminar abstract only, no write-up; unclear whether pieces are orthoschemes or non-obtuse simplices, and either way d=3 was already settled by Lenhard.

events.ai_basis: The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra, following the directions by the authors.

judgement.why: The classical results (d=2 through d=5) each settle one dimension of a question asked for every dimension, so they are cases, all before the snapshot; journal publication in Elemente der Mathematik, Geometriae Dedicata and Beiträge counts as digestion. Böhm's optimality of 12 is a bound on the count, not a new case. Orthoscheme-into-orthoscheme results (Debrunner, Brandts et al.) and the brick dissection change the question and are variants. After the snapshot nothing touches the question: Lénárt 2025 states no result for general simplices (none); Duhr-Mork's decomposition is signed by the paper's own eq. (9), so it is not a dissection (variant); Mork 2026 only restates it (none); Lotz and Norin-Steiner are different Hadwiger theorems (variant). The GPT-6 Astra credit is real for its own event, but that event is about graph colouring and is set aside as a variant.
judgement.doubts: The classical figures rest on Wikipedia; the originals were not read. The closest call is whether Duhr-Mork's decomposition is a genuine dissection. The paper says 'union of orthoschemes', but its explicit sign factor and Ren et al.'s statement that such triangulations are 'not a dissection' decide it as signed.
